deals_cleared.merger_description: Transocean Limited (**Transocean**) proposes to acquire Valaris Limited (**Valaris**) (the **Acquisition**) by way of merger, where Transocean shareholders will own approximately 53% of the combined entity and Valaris shareholders will own the remaining 47%.

events.title: Transocean - Valaris - Phase 1 determination
events.determination_commission_division: Determination made by Commissioner Williams pursuant to a delegation under section 25(1) of the Act

determination_table_content.details:
Transocean Limited (Transocean) proposes to acquire Valaris
Limited (Valaris) by way of merger (the Acquisition).

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has
determined under section 51ABZE(1) of the Competition and
Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) that the Acquisition may be put into effect.

The acquirer, Transocean, is a global provider of offshore contract
drilling services. Transocean’s fleet consists of 20 drillships (three of
which are cold stacked1) and seven semisubmersibles. In Australia,
Transocean currently has two semisubmersibles under contract and
a drillship due to commence operations in 2027.
The target, Valaris, is a global provider of offshore contract drilling
services. Valaris’ fleet consists of 13 drillships (three of which are
currently cold stacked), one semisubmersible (currently warm
stacked2) and 31 jackups (seven of which are currently cold or warm
stacked). In Australia, Valaris currently has one jackup under
contract.
The reasons for the ACCC’s determination are set out in section 2.

determination_statement_of_reasons.text: When making a determination in Phase 1, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) undertakes a competition assessment and considers whether it is appropriate for an acquisition to be approved or subject to further assessment in Phase 2 in accordance with section 51ABZJ of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) (the Act). In doing so, the ACCC must have regard to the object of the Act and all relevant matters, including the interests of consumers.
For more information about the ACCC’s approach to considering notified acquisitions, see the ACCC’s merger assessment guidelines and interim merger process guidelines.

In conducting its competition assessment, the ACCC has considered the information and documents that were submitted with the notification form, additional information provided by the parties to the acquisition, market feedback and publicly available information.

For the reasons given below, the ACCC has determined that the Acquisition may be put into effect. 1 Cold stacked rigs are in long term storage. 2 Warm stacked rigs are in short to medium term storage.
Industry background

Offshore contract drilling companies provide drilling services over the life of oil and gas projects, including exploration, appraisal and development drilling, workovers and plug and abandonment works. Customers of these services are typically oil and gas production companies who select providers through open or invitation-only tender processes.

Offshore contract drilling companies provide these services with mobile offshore drilling units (rigs), of which there are three main types, jackups, semisubmersibles and drillships. Jackups are typically used for drilling at relatively shallow waters, semisubmersibles in midwater and drillships in deep water or ultra deep water environments.

In addition to water depth, customers also have regard to sea and weather conditions at the drill site, technical requirements and past experience in selecting a rig type. The ACCC understands that customers typically identify a preferred rig type before seeking tenders from providers of offshore contract drilling service providers.

Offshore contract drilling companies also provide associated equipment and work crews along with rigs to customers. These components are typically included in a day-rate which includes the hire and operation of rigs. Australian customers can often be charged mobilisation fees to transport rigs from locations across the world to drill sites and demobilisation costs to transport rigs from drill sites to service other customers or to be stacked.
Stacking refers to temporarily taking a rig out of service and placing it into a state of storage and preservation. There are two types of stacking:

items: Warm stacking: refers to rigs in short to medium term storage, often with a full or almost full crew who conduct routine maintenance of the rig. Warm stacked rigs often incur ongoing costs; however, they can be deployed immediately or within days without incurring significant costs.

Cold stacking: refers to rigs in long term storage, often unmanned or with very minimal crew. Compared to warm stacked rigs, cold-stacked rigs take longer and incur higher costs to become deployable again.

determination_statement_of_reasons.text: Overlap between the Parties

Transocean and Valaris overlap in the supply of offshore contract drilling services. Both Parties provide these services via semisubmersibles and drillships, though Valaris appears to have limited presence in semisubmersibles, with only a single semisubmersible as part of its fleet.
Transocean and Valaris provide offshore contract drilling services in Australia and also globally.
Competition assessment

The ACCC has considered the effects of the Acquisition by comparing the likely future state of competition if the Acquisition proceeds against the continuation of the current state of competition (being the likely future state of competition if the Acquisition does not proceed).
Relevant areas of competition
The ACCC considered the competition effects of the Acquisition on the supply of semisubmersibles and drillships for offshore contract drilling in Australia.

In its assessment, the ACCC has had regard to the prevalence of drillships and semisubmersibles for projects in Australia. Based on customer feedback and tender data provided by the Parties, semisubmersibles appear to be the typically preferred rig type for offshore contract drilling in Australia over drillships, primarily for technical reasons.

For the purposes of this assessment, it was not necessary for the ACCC to form a concluded view on the precise scope of the affected market(s), because it does not materially alter the ACCC's competition assessment.
Competition effects in the supply of semisubmersibles

The ACCC considers the Acquisition is unlikely to have the effect of substantially lessening competition in relation to the supply of offshore contract drilling with semisubmersibles for Australian customers.

The ACCC considers that Transocean and Valaris are not presently close competitors in the supply of offshore contract drilling with semisubmersibles. Valaris has a single semisubmersible, which is currently warm stacked in Malaysia, and which does not appear to pose a significant competitive constraint on Transocean.

The ACCC also finds that post-Acquisition, the Parties would likely continue to be constrained by alternative suppliers of semisubmersibles for offshore contract drilling, including Noble, Seadrill and Stena Drilling.

In reaching these findings, the ACCC considered customer feedback and tender data which indicated the Parties currently do not pose a significant competitive constraint on each other for tender opportunities with Australian customers.
Competition effects in the supply of drillships

The ACCC considers the Acquisition is unlikely to have the effect of substantially lessening competition in relation to the supply of offshore contract drilling with drillships for Australian customers.

Though the Parties both have multiple drillships as part of their fleet, the ACCC notes that drillships appear to be less commonly used on Australian oil and gas projects and that Transocean and Valaris do not currently have drillships operating in Australia or in surrounding regions.

The ACCC considers that, following the Acquisition, the Parties would likely continue to be constrained by alternative suppliers of drillships for offshore contract drilling services and who operate globally and supply to Australian customers, including Noble, Saipem, Stena Drilling, and Vantage Drilling. These findings are based on information from the Parties and market feedback.

deals_cleared.merger_description: Kinetic Holding Company Pty Ltd (**Kinetic**) proposes to acquire 100% of the shares in L.C. Dyson’s Bus Services Pty Ltd (**Dysons**, together with its affiliates, the **Dysons Group**) pursuant to a share sale agreement.

events.title: Kinetic - Dysons - Phase 1 determination
events.determination_commission_division: Determination made by Commissioner Williams pursuant to a delegation under section 25(1) of the Act

determination_table_content.details:
Kinetic Holding Company Pty Ltd (Kinetic)’s proposed acquisition of:
• 100% of the shares in L.C. Dyson’s Bus Services Pty Ltd
(Dysons, together with its affiliates, the Dysons Group)
pursuant to a share sale agreement; and
• certain freehold and leasehold interests in bus depot assets
currently leased by the Dysons Group and owned by related
parties of Dysons’ shareholders (the Acquisition).

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has
determined under section 51ABZE(1) of the Competition and
Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) that the Acquisition may be put into effect.

The acquirer, Kinetic, is a transportation company that operates bus
services in Australia and overseas. These services include urban
route and school services, regional bus services, and charter bus
services, airport transfers bus services and some specialised bus
services, for example to the mining and resources sector.
Kinetic has operations in Victoria, New South Wales, Queensland,
Northern Territory, Western Australia and Tasmania.
In Victoria, Kinetic:
• supplies urban bus services in certain areas of metropolitan
Melbourne
• holds the head contract with Metro Trains for train
replacement services during planned disruptions in the
South-East area of Melbourne, and during unplanned
disruptions across Melbourne
• holds the head contract with Yarra Journey Makers for tram
replacement services
• supplies airport transfer and landside services via SkyBus
and some charter services in metropolitan Melbourne.
In regional NSW, Kinetic:
• operates urban and school bus services in the
Murwillumbah and Tweed Heads area
• supplies charter services from depots in Murwillumbah and
Tweed Heads.
The target, Dysons, is a family-owned coach and bus operator based
in Melbourne, which provides services in Victoria, regional New
South Wales and regional South Australia. These services include
urban route services, school services, regional bus services, rail
replacement services and charter services.
In Victoria, Dysons:
• supplies urban bus services in certain areas of metropolitan
Melbourne, and regional bus services in South-Eastern
Victoria (Gippsland and Sale) and North-Eastern Victoria
(Wangaratta, Wodonga and Shepparton)
• holds the head contract with Metro Trains for train
replacement services during planned disruptions in the
North-West area of Melbourne
• manages V/Line’s appointed subcontractors on V/Line’s
behalf to provide rail replacement services for regional rail
• supplies dedicated school services and charter services.
In NSW, Dysons supplies school bus services under contracts with
Transport for NSW in the Finley, Deniliquin, Hay, Moama and
Balranald areas. Dysons also provides some NSW transit
replacement services for NSW Trains.

determination_table_content.item:
Overlap and relationship
between the Parties
determination_table_content.details:
The Parties overlap in the supply of:
• urban bus services in Victoria, specifically Melbourne
• transit replacement services in Victoria
• regional bus services in New South Wales
• charter bus services in Melbourne.

When making a determination in Phase 1, the Australian Competition
and Consumer Commission (ACCC) undertakes a competition
assessment and considers whether it is appropriate for an
acquisition to be approved or subject to further assessment in
Phase 2 in accordance with section 51ABZJ of the Competition and
Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) (the Act). In doing so, the ACCC must have
regard to the object of the Act and all relevant matters, including the
interests of consumers.
For more information about the ACCC’s approach to considering
notified acquisitions, see the ACCC’s merger assessment guidelines
and interim merger process guidelines.
In conducting its competition assessment, the ACCC has considered
the information and documents that were submitted with the
notification form, information from third partes, and publicly
available information.
The ACCC has determined that the Acquisition may be put into
effect as it considers that the Acquisition is unlikely to have the
effect of substantially lessening competition in any market. In
reaching its decision, and based on the material before it, the ACCC
makes the following findings.
Supply of urban bus services in Victoria
• Kinetic would continue to face competition from alternative
credible bidders for urban bus service contracts in Victoria,
including from interstate and international operators.
• All assets required to operate urban bus services in Melbourne
are held by a special purpose vehicle and are transferable to an
incoming operator under the asset transfer provisions contained
in the Melbourne Bus Franchise and Melbourne Zero Emissions
Bus Franchise contracts, which limits the competitive advantage
of incumbents in future tenders.
• The Department of Transport and Planning, which supports the
Head, Transport for Victoria in carrying out its functions,
including the contracting of bus services in Victoria, has the
ability to structure tender processes in a way that promotes
competition.
Supply of transit replacement services in Victoria
• Some market participants raised concerns that the Acquisition
would reduce competition for head contracts and give rise to the
risk the merged entity could internalise or control subcontracting
opportunities.
• The Acquisition would be unlikely to reduce competition for head
contracts as these services are competitively tendered,
opportunities arise around every 3-5 years, public transport
operators have switched head contractors in the past, and
operators do not need local depots or compliant fleet vehicles to
hold head contracts.
• Kinetic would continue to face competition from alternative
credible bidders for head contracts for the coordination and
delivery of transit replacement services in Victoria.
• The merged entity would not have the ability or incentive to
foreclose rivals’ access to subcontractor work. Demand for
transit replacement services is highly volatile, it is unlikely that
any single operator could always fulfil demand, and most hours
have historically been subcontracted. Further, there are
contractual limitations on the use of urban bus fleet vehicles for
other purposes, which limits any advantage the merged entity
may have as an urban bus services supplier to provide transit
replacement work.
Supply of bus services in regional New South Wales
• The Parties have not competed for contracts in New South
Wales in the past and it is unlikely there would be significant
competition between the Parties in the absence of the
Acquisition.
Supply of charter bus services in Melbourne
• Kinetic would continue to face competition from alternative
suppliers of charter bus service providers in Melbourne.

A notifying party, or other person who has been allowed to do so by
the Australian Competition Tribunal, may apply for review if they are
dissatisfied with the determination. Pursuant to section 100C of the
Act, applications for review of the determination are to be made to
the Australian Competition Tribunal before the end of 14 calendar
days after this statement of reasons was included on the ACCC’s
Acquisitions Register. To confirm whether there has been any
application for review, please contact the Australian Competition
Tribunal.

events.title: Hewitt - Nolan Meats - Phase 1 determination
events.determination_commission_division: Determination made by Commissioner Williams pursuant to a delegation under section 25(1) of the Act

determination_table_content.details:
An entity within the Hewitt group (Hewitt), Sapphire Cattle
Company’s proposed acquisition of Nolan Meats Pty Ltd (Nolan
Meats), including land and assets, via connected entities
(the Acquisition).
Hewitt is a majority-owned subsidiary of the Public Sector Pension
Investment Board, an investment management fund established by
the Parliament of Canada. The remaining shares in Hewitt are owned
by the Hewitt family.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has
determined under section 51ABZE(1) of the Competition and
Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) that the Acquisition may be put into effect.

The acquirer, Hewitt, is a red meat producer, headquartered in
Brisbane, which farms cattle and sheep, undertakes secondary
processing of beef into value-added products (such as beef patties),
and distributes (including the packaging, marketing and sale of) beef
to supermarkets, the food service industry, butchers and
international customers. Hewitt predominantly produces organic
beef products.
The target, Nolan Meats, is a beef producer headquartered in
Gympie, Queensland. Nolan Meats undertakes lot feeding where
cattle are grain-fed, primary processing of cattle (initial slaughter
and carcass handling), and the wholesale distribution
(including packaging, marketing and sale) of beef to supermarkets,
the food service industry, butchers and international customers.
Nolan Meats’ core assets include a primary processing facility with
an annual capacity of 260,000 head of cattle, located in Gympie, and
a 4,000 standard cattle unit-licensed beef cattle feedlot situated 65
kilometres west of the processing facility.

determination_table_content.item:
Overlap and relationship
between the Parties
determination_table_content.details:
The parties overlap in the supply of fattened cattle and the supply of
wholesale and retail beef products to both domestic and export
customers.
The parties also have a vertical relationship, as Hewitt uses Nolan
Meats’ primary processing facility in Gympie, Queensland, to process
some of its fattened cattle.

When making a determination in Phase 1, the Australian Competition
and Consumer Commission (ACCC) undertakes a competition
assessment and considers whether it is appropriate for an
acquisition to be approved or subject to further assessment in
Phase 2 in accordance with section 51ABZJ of the Competition and
Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) (the Act). In doing so, the ACCC must have
regard to the object of the Act and all relevant matters, including the
interests of consumers.
For more information about the ACCC’s approach to considering
notified acquisitions, see the ACCC’s merger assessment guidelines
and interim merger process guidelines.
In conducting its competition assessment, the ACCC has considered
the information and documents that were submitted with the
notification form and information from third parties.
The ACCC has determined that the Acquisition may be put into
effect as it considers that the Acquisition is unlikely to have the
effect of substantially lessening competition in any market. In
reaching its decision, and based on the material before it, the ACCC
makes the following findings.
• The parties are not close competitors in the supply of
fattened cattle. Hewitt produces and acquires predominantly
organic, grass-fed fattened cattle, while Nolan Meats
acquires feeder cattle for grain finishing, on its own feedlot
and third party-contracted feedlots, to produce grain-fed
fattened cattle.
• The parties are not close competitors in the distribution of
beef products as Hewitt predominantly supplies organic
grass-fed and other ‘high claims’ certified beef products for
export (and to limited extent, domestically) and Nolan Meats
predominantly supplies beef products for domestic sale
(and to a limited extent, for export).
• Post-Acquisition, the merged entity would be unlikely to have
the ability and incentive to foreclose rival fattened cattle
suppliers’ access to primary processing services, as there
are multiple alternative primary processing service suppliers
available in the relevant region surrounding Nolan Meats’
Gympie processing facility.

A notifying party, or other person who has been allowed to do so by
the Australian Competition Tribunal, may apply for review if they are
dissatisfied with the determination. Pursuant to section 100C of the
Act, applications for review of the determination are to be made to
the Australian Competition Tribunal before the end of 14 calendar
days after this statement of reasons was included on the ACCC’s
Acquisitions Register. To confirm whether there has been any
application for review, please contact the Australian Competition
Tribunal.

events.title: INNIO Group - Enerflex Aftermarket Services - Questionnaire
events.display_title: INNIO Group - Enerflex Aftermarket Services - Questionnaire

events.title: INNIO Group – Enerflex - Phase 1 Determination - 27 July 2026
events.determination_commission_division: Determination made by Commissioner Williams pursuant to a delegation under section 25(1) of the Act

determination_table_content.details:
INNIO Group’s (INNIO) proposed acquisition of 100% of the share
capital in Enerflex Service Pty Limited (Enerflex Service), which
provides aftermarket services (spare parts, repair and maintenance)
for gas compression and energy infrastructure (the Acquisition).

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has
determined under section 51ABZE(1) of the Competition and
Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) that the Acquisition may be put into effect.

INNIO Holding GmbH (INNIO Holding), through its wholly owned
subsidiaries INNIO Jenbacher International B.V. and INNIO
Jenbacher Netherlands B.V. (together with their affiliates, the INNIO
Group) proposes to acquire 100% of the share capital in Enerflex
Service Pty Limited (Enerflex Service).
INNIO Group is a global manufacturer of gas power units under the
Jenbacher and Waukesha brands.
INNIO Group manufactures gas power units and genuine spare parts
at its facilities (primarily in Austria for Jenbacher, and the United
States and Canada for Waukesha) and supplies these globally
through distributors, including in Australia.
The target, Enerflex Service is an indirect, wholly owned subsidiary of
Enerflex Ltd (together with all its subsidiaries, Enerflex Group).
Enerflex Service is an aftermarket services provider for energy
infrastructure operators in Australia. It provides maintenance, repair,
replacement of spare parts, field services, retrofits, and the supply of
gas power units (new and refurbished as replacements) as part of
their aftermarket services for a wide variety of gas compression and
power generation units and other related equipment, such as
compressor units and electric motors.

determination_table_content.item:
Overlap and relationship
between the parties
determination_table_content.details:
The parties have a vertical relationship. Enerflex Service supplies
aftermarket services for Waukesha gas power units to owners and
operators of such units, and sources Waukesha spare parts and gas
power units from INNIO for owners and operators of such units.
INNIO does not provide aftermarket services and has no direct sales
of Waukesha spare parts or power units to Australia, and Enerflex
Australia does not manufacture power units.

When making a determination in Phase 1, the Australian Competition
and Consumer Commission (ACCC) undertakes a competition
assessment and considers whether it is appropriate for an
acquisition to be approved or subject to further assessment in
Phase 2 in accordance with section 51ABZJ of the Competition and
Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) (the Act). In doing so, the ACCC must have
regard to the object of the Act and all relevant matters, including the
interests of consumers.
For more information about the ACCC’s approach to considering
notified acquisitions, see the ACCC’s merger assessment guidelines
and interim merger process guidelines.
In conducting its competition assessment, the ACCC has considered
the information and documents that were submitted with the
notification form information from third partes, including
submissions expressing concerns that the Acquisition would lead to
reduced competitive tension in the supply of Waukesha spare parts
and/or foreclosure of rival aftermarket service suppliers who rely on
access to Waukesha spare parts.
The ACCC has determined that the Acquisition may be put into
effect as it considers that the Acquisition is unlikely to have the
effect of substantially lessening competition in any market. In
reaching its decision, and based on the material before it, the ACCC
makes the following findings:
• There is no horizontal overlap between INNIO and Enerflex
Service. INNIO does not provide aftermarket services and
has no direct sales of Waukesha spare parts or power units
to Australia and Enerflex Service does not manufacture
power units.
• There are a number of other OEM gas unit suppliers and
aftermarket service suppliers in Australia that compete in
the supply of gas compression power units and aftermarket
services for gas compression power units respectively.
• INNIO is unlikely to have requisite market power in
downstream aftermarket services markets or upstream OEM
gas unit markets to have the ability to foreclose its upstream
or downstream competitors by raising prices or reducing
service with respect to the supply of Waukesha spare parts
or aftermarket services to competitors.

A notifying party, or other person who has been allowed to do so by
the Australian Competition Tribunal, may apply for review if they are
dissatisfied with the determination. Pursuant to section 100C of the
Act, applications for review of the determination are to be made to
the Australian Competition Tribunal before the end of 14 calendar
days after this statement of reasons was included on the ACCC’s
Acquisitions Register. To confirm whether there has been any
application for review, please contact the Australian Competition
Tribunal.

determination_table_content.details:
Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SpaceX)’s proposed
acquisition, via its subsidiary, of acquire 100% of the shares in
Anysphere, Inc. (Anysphere) (the Acquisition).

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has
determined under section 51ABZE(1) of the Competition and
Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) that the Acquisition may be put into effect.

The acquirer, SpaceX, is the ultimate parent company of the SpaceX
group, which includes, among other businesses, X.AI Corp (xAI), an
artificial intelligence (AI) company, and X Corp., which owns and
operates the X social media platform (formerly Twitter). xAI
develops the Grok family of large language models and offers Grok
Build, a terminal-native AI coding tool, to Grok and X subscribers.
Grok Build currently runs on xAI’s Grok model family.
The target, Anysphere, develops and operates Cursor, an AI coding
tool used by software developers to write and review code with the
assistance of AI models. Cursor users can select from a range of
third-party large language models (including Grok models) or
Anysphere’s proprietary Composer model to power Cursor’s AI
assistant features. Composer is purpose-built for Cursor and is not
offered as a standalone model for other purposes.

SpaceX and Anysphere (together, the Parties) overlap in the supply
of AI large language models, and in the supply of AI coding tools.
Cursor users can use SpaceX’s Grok models to power Cursor’s AI
assistant features.

and Consumer Commission (ACCC) undertakes a competition
assessment and considers whether it is appropriate for an
acquisition to be approved or subject to further assessment in

Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) (the Act). In doing so, the ACCC must have
